passage: For two years after Swati walked out of our startup, I couldn't say her name without my jaw clenching. She'd left three weeks before a big client pitch, taking her half of the savings with her. I lost the client. I told the story to anyone who'd listen. Last winter, I heard from a friend that her father had been very ill at the time, and she'd needed the money for his treatment. She hadn't told me because she was ashamed. At first I was even angrier: why didn't she trust me? Then, slowly, something softened. I wrote her a message and deleted it five times. Finally I sent: "I heard about your father. I'm sorry. I'm not angry anymore. Santosh" She replied an hour later. We haven't fixed everything. But I sleep better.

Counsellor's note from Usha, after sessions with Sarita, 24.

Sarita came in months after her grandmother died. She had meant to visit that weekend but stayed back for an office deadline. She spoke of it as if it were a crime. "I chose work over her," she kept saying.

Over several sessions, we talked about what she knew at the time: her grandmother had seemed well, and the deadline had felt urgent. I asked her what she would say to a friend in the same place. She was quiet, then said, "I'd tell her it wasn't her fault."

Last week she brought a photo of her grandmother and said she'd started writing her letters. She said, "I'm trying to forgive myself. Some days I can."

Next step: continue, and ask about her support at home. — Usha

qa.q: Why had Sarita stayed back instead of visiting her grandmother?
qa.a: For an office deadline.

qa.q: What does Sarita's statement 'I chose work over her' reveal about her feelings?
qa.a: She blamed herself harshly, feeling guilt and resentment toward herself for missing the visit.

qa.q: How did Usha's question about a friend help Sarita?
qa.a: It helped her see her situation with the same kindness she'd offer someone else, easing her self-blame.

qa.q: How might Sarita's grandmother have seen the missed visit, if she could have?
qa.a: She'd likely understand and not want her granddaughter to carry such guilt. 🤍

grounding: A counsellor records a young woman gradually letting go of resentment toward herself after a loss.

Saturday night.

Saw Vidya at Chinki's wedding today. First time in six years.

In college, she spread that rumour about me and the professor. Totally false, but it followed me for two years. I hated her for it. I used to rehearse what I'd say if I ever saw her again.

Today she came up to me at the buffet. Older, tired. She said, "Lalit, I was jealous and stupid back then. I'm sorry." Just that.

I felt the old anger rise. Then I noticed I didn't want to carry it anymore. I'd been holding it longer than the rumour lasted.

I said, "Thank you for saying it." We talked about work for five minutes. Not friends. But the stone in my stomach is gone.

At the Dussehra fair in Bijnor, Deepak saw Wasim by the balloon seller and almost turned away.

Five years ago they had pooled savings to open a mobile repair shop. Wasim backed out a week before the lease, and Deepak lost his deposit. They had grown up in the same lane, climbed the same mango trees. Deepak had stopped using his name.

But lately the anger felt old, like a shoe too small. Each time he saw Wasim's father at the mosque gate, he felt his jaw tighten, and he was sick of it.

So he walked over. Wasim went pale. "Deepak, I…"

"I was angry for a long time," Deepak said. "I'm done with that now. Your father's looking thin. Is he well?"

Wasim's eyes filled. They bought two cups of tea and talked about the old trees.

qa.a: They had planned to open a mobile repair shop with pooled savings.

qa.q: Why did Deepak decide to speak to Wasim?
qa.a: The anger had started to feel old and uncomfortable, and he was tired of how it tightened his body whenever he saw Wasim's family.

qa.q: What went right in how Deepak approached Wasim?
qa.a: He named his anger honestly but briefly, then showed care for Wasim's father, which let the conversation move forward instead of reopening the old fight.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt when Deepak walked over?
qa.a: He went pale, which suggests guilt and fear of a confrontation, and then relief and emotion when Deepak offered peace.

Beatriz saw Amara across the bakery queue in Porto on a Saturday morning and nearly walked out.
Five years ago, when Beatriz's mother died, Amara hadn't come to the funeral. No call, no message. Beatriz had rehearsed a hundred angry speeches since.
Amara saw her. Her face went pale. They ended up outside on the cold steps with two coffees.
“I was a coward,” Amara said quietly. “My own mother was sick then. I couldn't face a funeral. That's not an excuse.”
Beatriz looked at the river for a long moment. She had carried this so long it had become part of her. She noticed she was tired of holding it.
“It hurt,” she said. “A lot.”
“I know.”
“I think I'd like to stop being angry.” She broke her pastry in half and held out one piece. Amara took it, eyes wet.

qa.a: They sat outside on the cold steps with two coffees.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling when she looked at the river?
qa.a: She felt the weight of years of resentment and realised she was tired of holding on to it.

qa.q: What helped this conversation lead to forgiveness?
qa.a: Amara admitted her failure without excuses, and Beatriz honestly said it had hurt before choosing to let go.

qa.q: How might Amara have felt when Beatriz held out half the pastry?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and grateful, moved that her old friend was willing to let go 🤍

Yamini had not stepped into the Kochi sports club's pavilion in three years, not since the final she lost for her team.
She had been the captain, twenty-two, and she had missed the penalty in the last minute. For three years she replayed it: her run-up, the keeper's hand. She quit hockey. She stopped answering the team group.
Now Jomon, who'd been in goal that season, had asked her to coach the under-14s on Saturdays.
She stood by the trophy cabinet. The photo of that team was still there. She looked at her own face, so young, so sure.
“You're allowed to stop punishing her,” Jomon said beside her.
Yamini laughed, and it came out shaky. “She was trying her best, wasn't she.”
“She was.”
She picked up the whistle from the desk. “Saturday, then. Seven?”

Dear Sunaina,
It's been six years since college, and I think it's time I wrote this.
When you told everyone in our hostel that I'd cheated in the second-year exam, it wasn't true, and you knew it. I lost friends. I stopped eating in the mess. For a long time I hated you with a kind of energy I'm not proud of.
When you sent that apology message last month, my first thought was to ignore it. I've read it maybe twenty times since.
I've decided I don't want to carry this anymore. It isn't because what you did was small. It wasn't. It's because I'm twenty-six and I'm tired of letting that year decide how I feel.
So I forgive you. I don't know yet if we'll be close again. But I'm putting this down.
Rashmi

qa.a: It's been six years since college.

passage: I'm Alka, Omkar's elder sister. When Omkar was twenty-four, his start-up failed. He'd convinced two school friends to invest their savings with him. They lost it all. For a year, he barely left his room. He was furious with himself, calling himself a fraud, refusing to meet those friends. Then something shifted. I saw him write two long letters, one to each friend, owning every mistake. He started paying them back in small amounts from his new job. One evening, I heard him on the phone, laughing with one of them for the first time. Later, on the terrace, he said, "I don't hate myself anymore, Didi. I made a big mistake. I'm not the mistake." I don't know how he got there, but I saw his shoulders drop that night.

Sarita, you want to know how I stopped hating my brother? Sit.
When I was twenty-four, our father left the house to him alone. I, Kashish, the elder daughter, the one who nursed Papa for two years, got nothing. I didn't speak to my brother for three years. I rehearsed arguments in the bath.

Her mother, Uma, didn't look up from the stove. "It was yours. From the hostel."
"The hostel you sent me to when I was ten. After Papa left."
Uma turned off the flame. "Madhuri. I was working two shifts. I didn't know what else to do."

Her younger brother Kunal, sitting at the table, stopped scrolling.

"I kept the letters. I never answered." Madhuri took a breath. "I've been talking to a counsellor. I don't want to carry this anymore. I'm not saying it didn't hurt. I'm saying I'm putting it down."
Uma's eyes filled. She reached out, then stopped. Madhuri stepped forward and held her.
Kunal quietly left the room.
